rationale: A wins because it is just as beat-shaped as B but has better brakes: "Without this proof, this is a question to prepare for, not an angle to pitch" keeps the labor angle honest. B has good instincts, especially "A grocery marketplace built a $1B ad business out of 6,000 brands," but it keeps wandering into unearned claims like "delivery growth has stalled" and "1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack." That is the difference between usable strategy and a clever memo that will make IR reach for the red pen.
gaps_in_A: "from a company that does not own a store" is likely true, but it is not in the supplied update. Source it or soften it to Instacart's retail-partner model.
"A retail-media desk writes on the milestone day or not at all" is too absolute. A $1B retail-media scale story can live longer if there is growth context or buyer proof.

"the one angle that needs no outside proof beyond the numbers you already hold" oversells readiness. The angle still needs run-rate methodology, exact order-growth period, and revenue mix before it is pitch-tight.
gaps_in_B: "delivery growth has stalled" overstates the facts. Single-digit growth is slowing, not stalled.
"slowing core, accelerating adjacency" invents acceleration. The update gives a $1B ad run rate, not ad growth rate or acceleration.

"Why 1,500 grocery banners are renting their tech stack instead of building it" is a seductive overreach. Partnership count does not prove renting, outsourcing, or use of carts/ad tech across those banners.
"ads on top" blurs the facts. The update says ads come from 6,000 brands and carts are expanding; it does not establish a bundled grocer tech stack.
